cor-complex-triangularizable.title: Complex Operators Are Triangularizable
cor-complex-triangularizable.html: Every operator on a finite-dimensional complex vector space V≠{0} is triangularizable over C. Every A∈Mn(C), n≥1, is similar to an upper triangular matrix in Mn(C).

cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable.title: Distinct Eigenvalues Imply Diagonalizable
cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V) have n distinct eigenvalues. Then T is diagonalizable. The same holds for A∈Mn(F) with n distinct eigenvalues in F.

cor-eigenspaces-direct-sum.title: Eigenspaces Form a Direct Sum
cor-eigenspaces-direct-sum.html: Let T∈L(V) and let λ1,…,λk∈F be distinct. Then the sum Eλ1(T)+⋯+Eλk(T) is direct. If V is finite-dimensional, then dim⁡Eλ1(T)+⋯+dim⁡Eλk(T)≤dim⁡V, and T has at most dim⁡V distinct eigenvalues.

cor-inverse-polynomial.title: The Inverse Is a Polynomial in the Matrix
cor-inverse-polynomial.title_html: The Inverse Is a Polynomial in the Matrix
cor-inverse-polynomial.html: Let n≥1, A∈Mn(F), and pA=xn+cn−1xn−1+⋯+c1x+c0. Then c0=(−1)ndetA. If A is invertible, then c0≠0 and A−1=−1c0(An−1+cn−1An−2+⋯+c2A+c1I). (For n=1 the bracket is I alone, and the formula reads A−1=−c0−1I.) The same holds for an invertible operator T on a space of dimension n≥1, with idV in place of I.

cor-minimal-divides-characteristic.title: The Minimal Polynomial Divides the Characteristic Polynomial
cor-minimal-divides-characteristic.title_html: The Minimal Polynomial Divides the Characteristic Polynomial
cor-minimal-divides-characteristic.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V).

  1. mT∣pT; in particular 1≤deg⁡mT≤n.
  2. If pT splits over F, say pT=(x−λ1)a1⋯(x−λk)ak with distinct λi, then mT=(x−λ1)s1⋯(x−λk)skwith 1≤si≤ai=aT(λi).

The same holds for A∈Mn(F) with mA and pA. In particular, over C, (b) applies to every A∈Mn(C).

cor-primary-components-dimension.title: Dimensions of the Primary Components
cor-primary-components-dimension.html: Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V≥1, T∈L(V), and suppose pT splits over F, with distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λk and mT=∏i(x−λi)si. Let Vi=ker(T−λiidV)si. Then pT|Vi=(x−λi)dim⁡Vianddim⁡Vi=aT(λi). Moreover Eλi(T)⊆Vi, with equality if and only if si=1.

cor-restriction-diagonalizable.title: Restrictions of Diagonalizable Operators
cor-restriction-diagonalizable.html: Let V be finite-dimensional, T∈L(V) diagonalizable, and U a T-invariant subspace. Then T|U is diagonalizable. Moreover U=⨁λ∈spec(T)(U∩Eλ(T)).

cor-trace-det-of-polynomial.title: Trace and Determinant of a Polynomial in T
cor-trace-det-of-polynomial.title_html: Trace and Determinant of a Polynomial in T
cor-trace-det-of-polynomial.html: Under the hypotheses of @thm-spectral-mapping, for every q∈F[x], trq(T)=q(λ1)+⋯+q(λn),detq(T)=q(λ1)⋯q(λn). In particular trTk=λ1k+⋯+λnk for every k∈N.

def-algebraic-multiplicity.title: Algebraic Multiplicity
def-algebraic-multiplicity.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V≥1, let T∈L(V) and λ∈F. The algebraic multiplicity of λ for T is aT(λ):=multλ(pT), the multiplicity of λ as a root of the characteristic polynomial (@def-root-multiplicity). For A∈Mn(F), aA(λ):=multλ(pA).

def-diagonalizable.title: Diagonalizable
def-diagonalizable.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F. An operator T∈L(V) is diagonalizable if there exists a basis B of V such that [T]B is a diagonal matrix.

A matrix A∈Mn(F) is diagonalizable over F if it is similar to a diagonal matrix: there exist an invertible P∈Mn(F) and a diagonal D∈Mn(F) with P−1AP=D, equivalently A=PDP−1.

def-eigenspace.title: Eigenspace
def-eigenspace.html: Let T∈L(V) and λ∈F. The eigenspace of T for λ is Eλ(T):=ker(T−λidV)={v∈V:Tv=λv}. For A∈Mn(F) we write Eλ(A)=Eλ(TA)=nul(A−λIn).

def-eigenvalue.title: Eigenvalue and Eigenvector
def-eigenvalue.html:
Let V be a vector space over F and T∈L(V). A scalar λ∈F is an eigenvalue of T if there exists a non-zero vector v∈V with Tv=λv. Every non-zero v∈V with Tv=λv is called an eigenvector of T for the eigenvalue λ.

For a matrix A∈Mn(F), the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A are those of TA:Fn→Fn: a scalar λ∈F and a non-zero v∈Fn with Av=λv.

def-geometric-multiplicity.title: Geometric Multiplicity
def-geometric-multiplicity.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, T∈L(V) and λ∈F. The geometric multiplicity of λ for T is gT(λ):=dim⁡Eλ(T)=dim⁡ker(T−λidV). For A∈Mn(F), gA(λ):=dim⁡Eλ(A)=n−rank(A−λIn).

def-invariant-subspace.title: Invariant Subspace
def-invariant-subspace.html: Let V be a vector space over F and T∈L(V). A subspace U of V is invariant under T, or T-invariant, if Tu∈Ufor every u∈U, that is, if T(U)⊆U.

def-left-eigenvector.title: Left Eigenvector
def-left-eigenvector.html: Let A∈Mn(F) and λ∈F. A left eigenvector of A for λ is a non-zero y∈Fn with yTA=λyT. To distinguish them, the eigenvectors of @def-eigenvalue are also called right eigenvectors.

def-markov-chain.title: Markov Chain, Steady State
def-markov-chain.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be stochastic. The Markov chain with transition matrix A and initial probability vector x0 is the sequence of probability vectors xk+1=Axk, that is, xk=Akx0. A steady state of A is a probability vector v with Av=v.

def-minimal-polynomial.title: Minimal Polynomial
def-minimal-polynomial.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F and T∈L(V). The minimal polynomial of T is the unique monic polynomial mT∈F[x] with IT={p∈F[x]:p(T)=0}=⟨mT⟩. Equivalently, mT is the monic polynomial of least degree with mT(T)=0.

For A∈Mn(F), the minimal polynomial is mA:=mTA: the monic polynomial of least degree with mA(A)=0.

def-restriction-operator.title: Restriction and Induced Operator
def-restriction-operator.html:
Let T∈L(V) and let U be a T-invariant subspace of V.

  1. The restriction of T to U is the operator T|U:U→U, u↦Tu.
  2. The induced operator (or quotient operator) on V/U is T¯:V/U→V/U, v+U↦Tv+U.

def-simultaneously-diagonalizable.title: Simultaneously Diagonalizable
def-simultaneously-diagonalizable.html: Let V be finite-dimensional. A family F⊆L(V) is simultaneously diagonalizable if there is one basis B of V such that [T]B is diagonal for every T∈F. Matrices A1,…,Ar∈Mn(F) are simultaneously diagonalizable over F if there is one invertible P∈Mn(F) with every P−1AiP diagonal.

def-spectrum.title: Spectrum
def-spectrum.html: Let T∈L(V). The spectrum of T is the set spec(T)⊆F of all eigenvalues of T. For A∈Mn(F), spec(A):=spec(TA).

def-stochastic-matrix.title: Stochastic Matrix, Probability Vector
def-stochastic-matrix.html:
Let n≥1.

  1. A vector x∈Rn is a probability vector if xi≥0 for every i and x1+⋯+xn=1.
  2. A matrix A∈Mn(R) is stochastic if every column of A is a probability vector: aij≥0 for all i,j, and ∑i=1naij=1 for every j.

def-triangularizable.title: Triangularizable
def-triangularizable.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F. An operator T∈L(V) is triangularizable over F if there exists a basis B of V such that [T]B is upper triangular. A matrix A∈Mn(F) is triangularizable over F if there exist an invertible P∈Mn(F) and an upper triangular U∈Mn(F) with P−1AP=U.

exm-diagonalize-3x3.title_html: Diagonalizing a 3×3 Matrix with a Repeated Eigenvalue
exm-diagonalize-3x3.html: Let A=(32−2−2−12−2−23)∈M3(R). Decide whether A is diagonalizable over R. If it is, find an invertible P and a diagonal D with P−1AP=D.

exm-fibonacci-binet.title: A Closed Formula for the Fibonacci Numbers
exm-fibonacci-binet.title_html: A Closed Formula for the Fibonacci Numbers
exm-fibonacci-binet.html: The Fibonacci numbers are defined by F0=0, F1=1 and Fk+2=Fk+1+Fk for k≥0. (Here Fk is a number, not a field; we work over R.) Find a formula for Fk by diagonalizing a 2×2 matrix.

exm-finite-order-diagonalizable.title: Complex Matrices of Finite Order Are Diagonalizable
exm-finite-order-diagonalizable.title_html: Complex Matrices of Finite Order Are Diagonalizable
exm-finite-order-diagonalizable.html: Let A∈Mn(C), n≥1, satisfy Ak=I for some k≥1. Show that A is diagonalizable, with eigenvalues among the k-th roots of unity. Show that both “over C” and “characteristic 0” matter.

exm-leslie-population.title: Three Age Classes
exm-leslie-population.html: A species is counted once a year in three age classes: young, juvenile and adult. Half of the young survive to become juveniles, and half of the juveniles survive to become adults; no adult survives another year. Each juvenile has on average 7/2 offspring and each adult 3. The Leslie matrix is L=(07/231/20001/20). Starting from x0=(20,10,5) (in hundreds of animals), find xk and describe the long-run growth and age distribution.

exm-minimal-polynomial-by-dependence.title: The Minimal Polynomial from the First Dependence
exm-minimal-polynomial-by-dependence.title_html: The Minimal Polynomial from the First Dependence
exm-minimal-polynomial-by-dependence.html: Find the minimal polynomial of A=(32−2−2−12−2−23)∈M3(R), the matrix of @exm-diagonalize-3x3, without using its eigenvalues.

exm-minimal-polynomial-by-eigenvalues.title: The Minimal Polynomial from the Eigenvalues

exm-primary-decomposition.title: A Primary Decomposition with an Irreducible Quadratic
exm-primary-decomposition.title_html: A Primary Decomposition with an Irreducible Quadratic
exm-primary-decomposition.html: Let C=(00210−1012)∈M3(R). Chapter 5 showed that its minimal polynomial is mC=(x−2)(x2+1) (@exr-polynomials-of-operators-b2). Find the primary decomposition of R3, the projections as polynomials in C, and the matrix of C in an adapted basis.

exm-repeated-root-recurrence.title: A Repeated Root
exm-repeated-root-recurrence.html: Over R, find all sequences with ak+2=4ak+1−4ak for every k∈N.

exm-rotation-invariant-subspaces.title: A Rotation Has No Invariant Lines
exm-rotation-invariant-subspaces.title_html: A Rotation Has No Invariant Lines
exm-rotation-invariant-subspaces.html: Let R:R2→R2, R(x,y)=(−y,x), be the rotation by a right angle. Find all R-invariant subspaces of R2.

exm-simultaneous-diagonalization.title: Diagonalizing Two Commuting Matrices Together
exm-simultaneous-diagonalization.html: Let A=(100−212−203),B=(1−220100−23)∈M3(R). Check that AB=BA, and find an invertible P such that P−1AP and P−1BP are both diagonal.

exm-spectral-mapping-3x3.title: A Polynomial in a Non-Diagonalizable Matrix
exm-spectral-mapping-3x3.title_html: A Polynomial in a Non-Diagonalizable Matrix
exm-spectral-mapping-3x3.html: Let A=(111201−332)∈M3(R), for which @exr-diagonalization-b1 found pA=(x+1)(x−2)2 and showed that A is not diagonalizable. Without computing any eigenvectors, find pA2, trA2 and detA2. Then find pq(A) for q=x2−x−2, and decide whether q(A)=0.

exm-third-order-recurrence.title: A Third-Order Recurrence
exm-third-order-recurrence.html: Find a formula for the sequence with a0=3, a1=2, a2=6 and ak+3=2ak+2+ak+1−2ak(k∈N).

exm-three-state-markov.title: Bicycles at Three Stations
exm-three-state-markov.html: A shared bicycle is parked each night at station 1, 2 or 3. The transition matrix is A=14(210121113); for instance a bicycle at station 3 stays there with probability 3/4 and never goes to station 1 in one night. Find Ak, its limit, and the long-run distribution of the bicycle.

exm-triangularize-3x3.title: Triangularizing a Matrix with a Single Eigenvector Line
exm-triangularize-3x3.title_html: Triangularizing a Matrix with a Single Eigenvector Line
exm-triangularize-3x3.html: Let A=(2010211−12)∈M3(R). Show that A is not diagonalizable but is triangularizable over R, and find an invertible P with P−1AP upper triangular.

exm-two-state-markov.title: A Two-State Chain
exm-two-state-markov.html: A machine is either working (state 1) or under repair (state 2) each day. A working machine is still working the next day with probability 9/10; a machine under repair is back to work the next day with probability 1/5. So the transition matrix is A=(9/101/51/104/5). Find Ak, its entrywise limit, and the long-run probability that the machine is working, if it is working on day 0.

exr-cayley-hamilton-a1.title: A1
exr-cayley-hamilton-a1.html:
1. State the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem for A∈Mn(F).
  2. True or false: deg⁡mA≤n for every A∈Mn(F), n≥1. Justify your answer.
  3. In one sentence, why is “pA(A)=det(AI−A)=0” not a proof?
  4. Suppose pA=(x−1)2(x+2). Which polynomials can mA be?
  5. True or false: if pA(A)=0, then pA is the minimal polynomial of A. Justify your answer.
  6. How do you write A−1 as a polynomial in A when A is invertible?

exr-cayley-hamilton-b1.title: B1: Inverse and a hundredth power
exr-cayley-hamilton-b1.title_html: B1: Inverse and a hundredth power
exr-cayley-hamilton-b1.html:
Let A=(3−210)∈M2(R).

  1. Find pA, and use the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem to compute A−1.
  2. Hence find A100 as a combination aA+bI, and write it as a matrix.

exr-cayley-hamilton-b2.title: B2: Trace zero in size two
exr-cayley-hamilton-b2.title_html: B2: Trace zero in size two
exr-cayley-hamilton-b2.html:
1. Let A∈M2(F) with trA=0. Prove that A2=−(detA)I.
  2. Deduce that for all X,Y∈M2(F), the matrix (XY−YX)2 is a scalar multiple of I.
  3. Show that the converse of (a) fails: give A∈M2(R) with A2 scalar and trA≠0.

exr-cayley-hamilton-b3.title: B3: Minimal polynomial from one product
exr-cayley-hamilton-b3.title_html: B3: Minimal polynomial from one product
exr-cayley-hamilton-b3.html: Each of the real matrices M1=(210020−113),M2=(200020−103) has characteristic polynomial (x−2)2(x−3). Find mM1 and mM2. Are M1 and M2 similar?

exr-cayley-hamilton-c1.title: C1: Cayley–Hamilton over a commutative ring
exr-cayley-hamilton-c1.title_html: C1: Cayley–Hamilton over a commutative ring
exr-cayley-hamilton-c1.html:
Let R be a commutative ring (the remark in Chapter 6, §4), and suppose, as for F[x], that the polynomials in x with coefficients in R form a commutative ring R[x] in which two polynomials are equal exactly when all their coefficients are equal. For A∈Mn(R), define pA=det(xI−A)∈R[x].

  1. Go through the proof of @thm-cayley-hamilton and name, for each step, the fact it uses. Explain why each fact holds over R and R[x], and conclude that pA(A)=0 for every A∈Mn(R).
  2. Let R=R[t] and A=(t1t20). Compute pA and verify pA(A)=0 directly.
  3. Let A∈Mn(Z) with detA=±1. Using (a) with R=Z, show that A−1 has integer entries.

exr-cayley-hamilton-c2.title: C2: The adjugate is a polynomial in the matrix
exr-cayley-hamilton-c2.title_html: C2: The adjugate is a polynomial in the matrix
exr-cayley-hamilton-c2.html:
Let n≥2, A∈Mn(F), pA=xn+cn−1xn−1+⋯+c0, and let B0,…,Bn−1 be as in the proof of @thm-cayley-hamilton.

  1. Using equation (2) of the proof, show that B0=An−1+cn−1An−2+⋯+c2A+c1I.
  2. Show that the constant matrix B0 equals adj(−A), and that adj(−A)=(−1)n−1adjA.
  3. Deduce that for every A∈Mn(F), invertible or not, adjA=(−1)n−1(An−1+cn−1An−2+⋯+c2A+c1I).
  4. Check (c) for S=(123246101), whose adjugate Chapter 6 computed (the warning after @cor-inverse-formula), given that pS=x3−6x2+2x.

exr-cayley-hamilton-c3.title: C3: Nilpotent matrices of size n
exr-cayley-hamilton-c3.title_html: C3: Nilpotent matrices of size n
exr-cayley-hamilton-c3.html:
Let F be any field, n≥1, and A∈Mn(F) with Ak=0 for some k≥1.

  1. Prove that mA=xs for some s with 1≤s≤n.
  2. Deduce that An=0.
  3. Give a 3×3 example with A2≠0, and explain why no 3×3 matrix has A3≠0=A4.

exr-commuting-operators-a1.title: A1
exr-commuting-operators-a1.html:
1. State the theorem relating commuting operators and eigenspaces.
  2. True or false: if ST=TS, then every eigenvector of T is an eigenvector of S. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: any two commuting matrices in M2(R) have a common eigenvector in R2. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A,B∈Mn(F) are simultaneously diagonalizable, then AB=BA. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if AB=BA and A is diagonalizable, then B is diagonalizable. Justify your answer.
  6. In the proof of @thm-simultaneous-diagonalization, which hypothesis makes each eigenspace of T invariant under S, and which makes the restriction of S diagonalizable?

exr-commuting-operators-b1.title: B1: Common eigenvectors
exr-commuting-operators-b1.html:
Let A=(1000101−12),B=(210−1402−25)∈M3(R).

  1. Verify that AB=BA.
  2. Find every common eigenvector of A and B.
  3. Hence show that A and B are not simultaneously diagonalizable, and explain which hypothesis of @thm-simultaneous-diagonalization fails.

exr-commuting-operators-b2.title: B2: Decide simultaneous diagonalizability
exr-commuting-operators-b2.html:
For each pair of real matrices, determine whether they are simultaneously diagonalizable over R. If they are, find a suitable P. Justify your answer.

  1. A=(1221), B=(0110).
  2. A=(1102), B=(1002).
  3. A=(2002), B=(2102).

exr-commuting-operators-b3.title: B3: Matrices commuting with a diagonal matrix
exr-commuting-operators-b3.title_html: B3: Matrices commuting with a diagonal matrix
exr-commuting-operators-b3.html:
1. Let D=diag(1,2,3)∈M3(R). Prove that a matrix B∈M3(R) commutes with D if and only if B is diagonal.
  2. Let D′=diag(1,1,2)∈M3(R). Describe all B∈M3(R) with BD′=D′B, and find one that is not diagonalizable.

exr-commuting-operators-c1.title: C1: The commutant of a matrix with distinct eigenvalues
exr-commuting-operators-c1.title_html: C1: The commutant of a matrix with distinct eigenvalues
exr-commuting-operators-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(F), n≥1, have n distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λn∈F.

  1. Prove that if AB=BA, then B is diagonalizable and every eigenvector of A is an eigenvector of B.
  2. Prove that if AB=BA, then B=q(A) for some q∈F[x] of degree at most n−1.
  3. Deduce that {B∈Mn(F):AB=BA} is a subspace of Mn(F) of dimension n, with basis (I,A,…,An−1).

Hint: for (b), use Lagrange interpolation.

exr-commuting-operators-c2.title: C2: Commuting nilpotent matrices
exr-commuting-operators-c2.html:
Recall that N∈Mn(F) is nilpotent if Na=0 for some a≥1 (@exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-c2). Let N,M∈Mn(F) with NM=MN, Na=0 and Mb=0 for some a,b≥1.

  1. Prove that NM is nilpotent.
  2. Prove that (N+M)a+b−1=0, so that N+M is nilpotent.
  3. Show that both conclusions can fail without NM=MN.
  4. Now let F=C. Give a second proof of (b) using @thm-simultaneous-triangularization.

Hint: for (b), expand the power as a sum of products of a+b−1 factors, each equal to N or M.

exr-diagonalization-a1.title: A1
exr-diagonalization-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for A∈Mn(F) to be diagonalizable over F.
  2. State the Diagonalization Theorem, with at least four equivalent conditions.
  3. True or false: a diagonalizable n×n matrix has n distinct eigenvalues. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: every invertible matrix is diagonalizable. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: every diagonalizable matrix is invertible. Justify your answer.
  6. If P−1AP=D is diagonal, what are the columns of P, and how are they matched with the diagonal of D?

exr-diagonalization-b1.title: B1: Diagonalize or show impossible
exr-diagonalization-b1.html:
For each real matrix, either find an invertible P and a diagonal D with P−1AP=D, or show that none exist.

  1. A1=(01−65).
  2. A2=(111201−332).
  3. A3=(−12−2−23−22−23).

exr-diagonalization-b2.title: B2: A tenth power
exr-diagonalization-b2.html:
Let A=(1221)∈M2(R).

  1. Diagonalize A.
  2. Hence find a formula for Ak, k∈N, and compute A10.

exr-diagonalization-b3.title: B3: A matrix with a parameter
exr-diagonalization-b3.title_html: B3: A matrix with a parameter
exr-diagonalization-b3.html: For t∈R, let At=(1100t0002). Determine all t for which At is diagonalizable over R. Justify your answer.

exr-diagonalization-c1.title: C1: Matrices with A^k = I
exr-diagonalization-c1.title_html: C1: Matrices with Ak=I
exr-diagonalization-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(C), n≥1, and k≥1.

  1. Prove that if Ak=I, then every eigenvalue λ of A satisfies λk=1.
  2. Prove that if A is diagonalizable and every eigenvalue satisfies λk=1, then Ak=I.
  3. Show that the hypothesis “diagonalizable” in (b) cannot be dropped.

exr-diagonalization-c2.title: C2: Polynomials of diagonalizable matrices
exr-diagonalization-c2.html:
1. Prove that if A∈Mn(F) is diagonalizable over F, then so is p(A) for every p∈F[x], and that every eigenvalue of p(A) has the form p(λ) with λ∈spec(A).
  2. Show that the converse of the first statement fails: find a non-diagonalizable A and a polynomial p with p(A) diagonalizable.

exr-diagonalization-c3.title: C3: The transpose map on M_n(F)
exr-diagonalization-c3.title_html: C3: The transpose map on Mn(F)
exr-diagonalization-c3.html:
Let n≥1 and τ:Mn(F)→Mn(F), τ(X)=XT.

  1. Suppose the characteristic of F is not 2. Prove that τ is diagonalizable, and find dim⁡E1(τ) and dim⁡E−1(τ).
  2. Under the same hypothesis, deduce pτ, trτ and detτ.
  3. Now let F=F2 and n≥2. Prove that τ is not diagonalizable.

Hint: for the dimensions, use the matrices Eij+Eji and Eij−Eji.

exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-a1.title: A1
exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-a1.html:
1. Define eigenvalue, eigenvector and eigenspace of an operator T∈L(V).
  2. True or false: 0 is an eigenvector of every operator. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: if 0 is an eigenvalue of A∈Mn(F), then A is not invertible. Justify your answer.
  4. State four conditions equivalent to “λ is an eigenvalue of T” for an operator on a finite-dimensional space V≠{0}.
  5. True or false: every operator on R2 has an eigenvalue. Justify your answer.
  6. True or false: the eigenvalues of A are the diagonal entries of a row echelon form of A. Justify your answer.

exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-b1.title: B1: Computing eigenvalues and eigenspaces
exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-b1.html:
Find the eigenvalues and a basis of each eigenspace of the following real matrices.

  1. A=(54−2−1).
  2. B=(201−1312−21).

Hence write down a basis of R2 consisting of eigenvectors of A, and a basis of R3 consisting of eigenvectors of B.

exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-b2.title: B2: The transpose map
exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-b2.html:
Let F be a field of characteristic not 2, and let τ:M2(F)→M2(F), τ(X)=XT.

  1. Show that every eigenvalue λ of τ satisfies λ2=1.
  2. Find spec(τ), and describe E1(τ) and E−1(τ) with a basis of each.

exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-b3.title: B3: Eigenvalues of powers and inverses
exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-b3.title_html: B3: Eigenvalues of powers and inverses
exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-b3.html:
Let T∈L(V) and let v be an eigenvector of T for λ.

  1. Prove that v is an eigenvector of T2 for λ2, and more generally of p(T) for p(λ), for every p∈F[x].
  2. Suppose T is invertible. Prove that λ≠0 and that v is an eigenvector of T−1 for λ−1.
  3. Show that the converse of the first statement in (a) fails: give T∈L(R2) such that −1 is an eigenvalue of T2 but T has no eigenvalue.

exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-c1.title: C1: Every vector an eigenvector
exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-c1.html:
Let V be a vector space over F and T∈L(V). Suppose every non-zero vector of V is an eigenvector of T. Prove that T=cidV for some c∈F.

Hint: compare the eigenvalues of v, w and v+w.

exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-c2.title: C2: Nilpotent operators
exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-c2.html:
An operator T∈L(V) is nilpotent if Tk=0 for some integer k≥1.

  1. Let V≠{0} and T nilpotent. Prove that spec(T)={0}. (No finite dimension is needed.)
  2. Let A∈Mn(C), n≥1, be nilpotent. Deduce that pA(x)=xn.
  3. Let A∈Mn(F), n≥1, be nilpotent. Prove that I+A is invertible.

exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-c3.title: C3: Real matrices of odd size
exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-c3.title_html: C3: Real matrices of odd size
exr-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors-c3.html:
1. Prove that every A∈Mn(R) with n odd has a real eigenvalue.
  2. Deduce that every operator on a real vector space of dimension 3 has an invariant line.
  3. Show that (a) fails for n=4: find A∈M4(R) with no real eigenvalue.

exr-invariant-subspaces-a1.title: A1
exr-invariant-subspaces-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for a subspace U of V to be invariant under T∈L(V).
  2. True or false: for every T∈L(V), the subspaces kerT and imT are T-invariant. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: if U is T-invariant, then Tu=u for every u∈U. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if U is invariant under S and under T, then U is invariant under S+T and under ST. Justify your answer.
  5. For v≠0, what condition on Tv makes span(v) invariant?
  6. In a basis whose first k vectors form a basis of a T-invariant subspace U, which block of [T]B is zero, and what are the two diagonal blocks?

exr-invariant-subspaces-b1.title: B1: All invariant subspaces of a diagonal matrix
exr-invariant-subspaces-b1.title_html: B1: All invariant subspaces of a diagonal matrix
exr-invariant-subspaces-b1.html: Let A=diag(1,2) act on R2. Find all A-invariant subspaces of R2.

exr-invariant-subspaces-b2.title: B2: Kernels of T - c\,\id
exr-invariant-subspaces-b2.title_html: B2: Kernels of T−cid
exr-invariant-subspaces-b2.html:
Let T∈L(V) and c∈F.

  1. Prove directly from the definition that ker(T−cidV) is T-invariant.
  2. Hence show that every subspace of ker(T−cidV) is T-invariant.

exr-invariant-subspaces-b3.title: B3: Invariance under differentiation
exr-invariant-subspaces-b3.html:
Let D be differentiation on V=R[x]≤3. Determine which of the following subspaces are D-invariant. Justify your answer.

  1. U1=span(1,x).
  2. U2=span(x,x2).
  3. U3={p∈V:p(0)=0}.
  4. U4=span(x2+2x, 2x+2, 2).
  5. U5=span(1,x2), the even polynomials in V.

exr-invariant-subspaces-c1.title: C1: A chain of invariant subspaces
exr-invariant-subspaces-c1.title_html: C1: A chain of invariant subspaces
exr-invariant-subspaces-c1.html:
Let F be any field and N=(010001000)∈M3(F), acting on F3, so Ne1=0, Ne2=e1, Ne3=e2. Put W0={0}, W1=span(e1), W2=span(e1,e2), W3=F3.

  1. Show that each Wj is N-invariant.
  2. Let U be an N-invariant subspace, and let j be the largest index such that some vector of U has a non-zero j-th entry (put j=0 if U={0}). Prove that U=Wj.
  3. Deduce that the N-invariant subspaces are exactly W0⊂W1⊂W2⊂W3, and that any two of them are comparable under inclusion.

Hint: for (b), apply N and N2 to a vector with non-zero j-th entry.

exr-invariant-subspaces-c2.title: C2: Invariance under the inverse
exr-invariant-subspaces-c2.html:
1. Let V be finite-dimensional, T∈L(V) invertible, and U a T-invariant subspace. Prove that T(U)=U, and deduce that U is T−1-invariant.
  2. Show that (a) fails without finite dimension. On V=FZ, the space of all functions Z→F written as two-sided sequences (sn)n∈Z, let (Ss)n=sn−1. Show that S is invertible, that U={s:sn=0 for all n<0} is S-invariant, and that U is not S−1-invariant.

Hint: for (a), consider the restriction T|U and its kernel.

exr-minimal-polynomial-a1.title: A1
exr-minimal-polynomial-a1.html:
1. Define the minimal polynomial of an operator T on a finite-dimensional space, and give its two equivalent descriptions.
  2. True or false: mA=pA for every A∈Mn(F). Justify your answer.
  3. State the relation between the roots of mT and the eigenvalues of T.
  4. Let A≠0 satisfy A3=0. Which polynomials can mA be?
  5. True or false: if mA=mB, then A∼B. Justify your answer.
  6. Explain why multiplication by x on F[x] has no minimal polynomial.

exr-minimal-polynomial-b1.title: B1: Computing minimal polynomials
exr-minimal-polynomial-b1.html:
Find the minimal polynomial of each real matrix.

  1. A1=(4−112).
  2. A2=(111111111).
  3. A3=(21101−1−1−11), given that pA3=(x−1)2(x−2).
  4. A4=(211−10−1112), given that pA4=(x−1)2(x−2).

Hence decide whether A3 and A4 are similar.

exr-minimal-polynomial-b2.title: B2: Operators with T^2 = T
exr-minimal-polynomial-b2.title_html: B2: Operators with T2=T
exr-minimal-polynomial-b2.html:
Let V≠{0} be finite-dimensional and T∈L(V) with T2=T.

  1. Show that mT∈{x, x−1, x(x−1)}.
  2. Show that mT=x exactly when T=0, and mT=x−1 exactly when T=idV.
  3. What is mT on V={0}?

exr-minimal-polynomial-b3.title: B3: Companion matrices
exr-minimal-polynomial-b3.html:
Let n≥2, p=xn+an−1xn−1+⋯+a1x+a0∈F[x], and let C=C(p) be its companion matrix (@exr-characteristic-polynomial-c1).

  1. Show that Cek=ek+1 for 1≤k≤n−1, so Cke1=ek+1 for 0≤k≤n−1.
  2. Deduce that no non-zero polynomial of degree less than n annihilates C.
  3. Show that p(C)e1=0, and hence p(C)ek+1=0 for all k≤n−1.
  4. Deduce that mC=p=pC.

exr-minimal-polynomial-c1.title: C1: Cyclic vectors
exr-minimal-polynomial-c1.html:
Let dim⁡V=n≥1 and T∈L(V). A vector v is a cyclic vector for T if (v,Tv,…,Tn−1v) is a basis of V.

  1. Prove that if T has a cyclic vector, then deg⁡mT≥n.
  2. Suppose v is cyclic and Tnv=−(a0v+a1Tv+⋯+an−1Tn−1v). Show that the matrix of T in the basis (v,…,Tn−1v) is the companion matrix of p=xn+an−1xn−1+⋯+a0 (for n≥2), and deduce mT=pT=p.
  3. Find a cyclic vector for J=(1101), and show that I2 has none.

(The converse of (a), that deg⁡mT=n forces a cyclic vector, is proved in Chapter 9.)

exr-minimal-polynomial-c2.title: C2: Minimal polynomials of the pieces
exr-minimal-polynomial-c2.title_html: C2: Minimal polynomials of the pieces
exr-minimal-polynomial-c2.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional, T∈L(V), and U a T-invariant subspace, with restriction T|U and induced operator T¯ on V/U (@def-restriction-operator).

  1. Prove that p(T|U)=p(T)|U and p(T¯)(v+U)=p(T)v+U for every p∈F[x].
  2. Deduce that mT|U∣mT and mT¯∣mT.
  3. Prove that mT∣mT|UmT¯.
  4. For J=(1101) and U=span(e1), compute all three minimal polynomials, and show that mT need not equal lcm(mT|U,mT¯).

Hint: for (c), apply mT¯(T) to v and ask where the result lies.

exr-multiplicities-a1.title: A1
exr-multiplicities-a1.html:
1. Define the algebraic and the geometric multiplicity of λ∈F for A∈Mn(F).
  2. State the inequality between them for an eigenvalue λ, and name the tool its proof uses.
  3. True or false: if a(λ)=1, then g(λ)=1. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: for every A∈Mn(C), the geometric multiplicities of the eigenvalues add up to n. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if A,B∈Mn(F) have the same characteristic polynomial, then gA(λ)=gB(λ) for every λ. Justify your answer.
  6. For A∈M3(C) with eigenvalues 2 (algebraic multiplicity 2) and −1, what are trA and detA?

exr-multiplicities-b1.title: B1: Computing multiplicities
exr-multiplicities-b1.html:
For each real matrix, find every eigenvalue together with its algebraic and geometric multiplicity.

  1. A1=(4−112).
  2. A2=(21101−1−1−11).
  3. A3=(211−10−1112), given that pA3=pA2.
  4. The matrix of the operator S(q)(x)=q(x+1) on R[x]≤2, in the basis (1,x,x2).

exr-multiplicities-b2.title: B2: A parameter that merges eigenvalues
exr-multiplicities-b2.title_html: B2: A parameter that merges eigenvalues
exr-multiplicities-b2.html: For t∈R, let At=(t1−13). Find all t for which At has a real eigenvalue λ with g(λ)<a(λ).

exr-multiplicities-b3.title: B3: Eigenvalues from trace and determinant
exr-multiplicities-b3.title_html: B3: Eigenvalues from trace and determinant
exr-multiplicities-b3.html:
1. Let A∈M3(R) have the eigenvalue 1+i (as a complex matrix) and detA=6. Find all eigenvalues of A over C, and trA.
  2. Let B∈M2(R) with trB=6 and detB=9. Show that spec(B)={3} with a(3)=2. Give one such B with g(3)=2 and one with g(3)=1.

exr-multiplicities-c1.title: C1: Nilpotent matrices
exr-multiplicities-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(C), n≥1, be nilpotent (Ak=0 for some k≥1).

  1. Prove that a(0)=n and g(0)=n−rankA.
  2. Deduce that g(0)=a(0) if and only if A=0.
  3. For N=(0100001000010000), check that N4=0 and compute g(0). How large can a(0)−g(0) be for a nilpotent n×n matrix?

exr-multiplicities-c2.title: C2: Multiplicities do not determine similarity
exr-multiplicities-c2.title_html: C2: Multiplicities do not determine similarity
exr-multiplicities-c2.html:
Let M1=(1100010000110001),M2=(1100011000100001)∈M4(R).

  1. Show that M1 and M2 have the same eigenvalues with the same algebraic and geometric multiplicities.
  2. Compute rank(M1−I)2 and rank(M2−I)2. Deduce that M1≁M2.
  3. Construct a matrix M∈M4(R) with spec(M)={2,5}, a(2)=3, g(2)=1, and a(5)=g(5)=1.

Hint: for (b), if B=P−1AP, relate (B−I)2 to (A−I)2.

exr-powers-recurrences-markov-a1.title: A1
exr-powers-recurrences-markov-a1.html:
1. Define a stochastic matrix, and say which convention (rows or columns) this book uses.
  2. True or false: for every stochastic A, the powers Ak converge entrywise. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: 1 is a right eigenvector of every stochastic matrix. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: every stochastic matrix is invertible. Justify your answer.
  5. Write down the general solution of ak+2=5ak+1−6ak over R.
  6. In @thm-linear-recurrence-solution, what are the numbers c1,…,cn?

exr-powers-recurrences-markov-b1.title: B1: Two recurrences
exr-powers-recurrences-markov-b1.html:
1. Solve ak+2=ak+1+2ak with a0=0, a1=3.
  2. Solve ak+2=6ak+1−9ak with a0=1, a1=6, by the method of @exm-repeated-root-recurrence.

exr-powers-recurrences-markov-b2.title: B2: A three-state chain
exr-powers-recurrences-markov-b2.html:
Let A=(1/21/21/41/401/41/41/21/2).

  1. Verify that A is stochastic, and find its steady state.
  2. Verify that (−1,0,1) and (1,−2,1) are eigenvectors of A, and find their eigenvalues.
  3. Hence find the entrywise limit of Ak, and the limit of the chain started at x0=e2.

exr-powers-recurrences-markov-b3.title: B3: The limit of a matrix power
exr-powers-recurrences-markov-b3.title_html: B3: The limit of a matrix power
exr-powers-recurrences-markov-b3.html:
Let A=(01−1/23/2)∈M2(R).

  1. Diagonalize A, and find a formula for Ak.
  2. Find the entrywise limit of Ak.
  3. Hence find limk→∞ak for the sequence with ak+2=32ak+1−12ak, in terms of a0 and a1.

exr-powers-recurrences-markov-c1.title: C1: Eigenvalues of a stochastic matrix
exr-powers-recurrences-markov-c1.title_html: C1: Eigenvalues of a stochastic matrix
exr-powers-recurrences-markov-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be stochastic, regarded as a complex matrix, and let λ∈C be an eigenvalue of A.

  1. Prove that |λ|≤1.
  2. Refine the argument: prove that |λ−aii|≤1−aii for some index i.
  3. Deduce that if every diagonal entry of A is positive, then −1 is not an eigenvalue of A.
  4. Show by an example that (c) fails if a diagonal entry is 0.

Hint: take a left eigenvector y for λ and an index i with |yi| as large as possible.

exr-powers-recurrences-markov-c2.title: C2: Two-state chains
exr-powers-recurrences-markov-c2.html:
Let 0≤p,q≤1 and A=(1−pqp1−q).

  1. Show that A is stochastic, with eigenvalues 1 and 1−p−q.
  2. Suppose 0<p+q<2. Prove that Ak converges entrywise, and find the limit and the steady state.
  3. In particular, if A has no zero entry, then Ak converges. What happens when p+q=0 and when p+q=2?

exr-primary-decomposition-a1.title: A1
exr-primary-decomposition-a1.html:
1. State the Primary Decomposition Theorem.
  2. State the criterion for diagonalizability in terms of the minimal polynomial.
  3. True or false: if mA=x(x−1)(x+1) over Q, then A is diagonalizable over Q. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A∈Mn(R) and Ak=I for some k≥1, then A is diagonalizable over R. Justify your answer.
  5. Let mT=(x−2)2(x+1). What are the summands of the primary decomposition, and is T diagonalizable?
  6. True or false: the restriction of a diagonalizable operator to an invariant subspace is diagonalizable. Justify your answer.

exr-primary-decomposition-b1.title: B1: Diagonalizable or not?
exr-primary-decomposition-b1.html:
Determine whether each matrix is diagonalizable over the given field. Justify your answer.

  1. A1=(211−10−1112) over R (see @exr-minimal-polynomial-b1).
  2. M1=(210020−113) over R (see @exr-cayley-hamilton-b3).
  3. Any A∈M5(Q) with A3=4A.
  4. Any A∈M2(R) with A2+I=0, over R and over C.

exr-primary-decomposition-b2.title: B2: Decomposing \nR^3
exr-primary-decomposition-b2.title_html: B2: Decomposing R3
exr-primary-decomposition-b2.html:
Let A=(21101−1−1−11)∈M3(R), which has mA=(x−1)2(x−2) (@exr-minimal-polynomial-b1 (c)).

  1. Find bases of V1=ker(A−I)2 and V2=ker(A−2I), and check that R3=V1⊕V2.
  2. Compare V1 with E1(A).
  3. Using (x−1)2−x(x−2)=1, write the two projections as polynomials in A, and compute them.
  4. Write the matrix of TA in the basis formed by your bases of V1 and V2.

exr-primary-decomposition-b3.title: B3: Matrices with A^3 = A
exr-primary-decomposition-b3.title_html: B3: Matrices with A3=A
exr-primary-decomposition-b3.html:
Let F have characteristic not 2, and let A∈Mn(F), n≥1, satisfy A3=A.

  1. Prove that A is diagonalizable, with spec(A)⊆{0,1,−1}.
  2. Now let F=R. Prove that rankA=tr(A2).

exr-primary-decomposition-c1.title: C1: A^p = A over \nF_p
exr-primary-decomposition-c1.title_html: C1: Ap=A over Fp
exr-primary-decomposition-c1.html:
Let p be a prime and A∈Mn(Fp), n≥1, with Ap=A.

  1. Let a∈Fp be non-zero. Show that b↦ab is a bijection of Fp∖{0}, and deduce ap−1=1. Conclude that ap=a for every a∈Fp.
  2. Deduce that xp−x=∏a∈Fp(x−a) in Fp[x].
  3. Prove that A is diagonalizable over Fp.
  4. Show that J=(1101) satisfies Jp=I over Fp but is not diagonalizable, and explain why this does not contradict (c).

Hint: for (a), compare the product of all non-zero elements with the product of all their multiples by a.

exr-primary-decomposition-c2.title: C2: Irreducible minimal polynomials
exr-primary-decomposition-c2.html:
Let V≠{0} be finite-dimensional, T∈L(V), and suppose mT is irreducible, of degree d. For v∈V, let Wv={q(T)v:q∈F[x]}.

  1. Show that Wv is the smallest T-invariant subspace of V containing v.
  2. Let v≠0. Prove that (v,Tv,…,Td−1v) is a basis of Wv. In particular dim⁡Wv=d.
  3. Deduce that the only T-invariant subspaces of Wv are {0} and Wv.
  4. Prove that V is a direct sum of subspaces of the form Wv, and hence that d divides dim⁡V.
  5. Illustrate with the rotation R of R2 and with R⊕R on R4.

Hint: for (b), use the gcd of mT with a polynomial of degree less than d. For (d), take a direct sum Wv1⊕⋯⊕Wvs that is as large as possible.

exr-spectral-mapping-a1.title: A1
exr-spectral-mapping-a1.html:
1. State the Spectral Mapping Theorem, including its hypothesis on pT.
  2. True or false: for every A∈Mn(R), every real eigenvalue of A2 is the square of a real eigenvalue of A. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: if A∈M2×3(F) and B∈M3×2(F), then pAB=pBA. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: for all A,B∈Mn(F), AB is similar to BA. Justify your answer.
  5. Define a left eigenvector of A∈Mn(F), and say how left eigenvectors of A are related to AT.
  6. True or false: a matrix A∈M3(C) with trA=trA2=trA3=0 satisfies A3=0. Justify your answer.

exr-spectral-mapping-b1.title: B1: Eigenvalues of a polynomial in A
exr-spectral-mapping-b1.title_html: B1: Eigenvalues of a polynomial in A
exr-spectral-mapping-b1.html:
Let A∈M3(C) have pA=(x−1)2(x+2).

  1. Find pA2+A+I, tr(A2+A+I) and det(A2+A+I). Is A2+A+I invertible?
  2. Find pA2+A−2I. Hence show that A2+A−2I is nilpotent.
  3. Find trA5 and det(A−1).

exr-spectral-mapping-b2.title: B2: AB and BA for a 2 \times 3 example
exr-spectral-mapping-b2.title_html: B2: AB and BA for a 2×3 example
exr-spectral-mapping-b2.html:
Let A=(101020) and B=(100−111).

  1. Compute AB, BA, pAB and pBA, and verify that x3pAB=x2pBA.
  2. Hence list the eigenvalues of BA without further computation, and find an eigenvector of BA for each non-zero eigenvalue by applying B to eigenvectors of AB.

exr-spectral-mapping-b3.title: B3: Left eigenvectors of a 2 \times 2 matrix
exr-spectral-mapping-b3.title_html: B3: Left eigenvectors of a 2×2 matrix
exr-spectral-mapping-b3.html:
Let A=(01−65)∈M2(R), whose right eigenvectors (1,2) for 2 and (1,3) for 3 were found in @exr-diagonalization-b1.

  1. Find a left eigenvector of A for each eigenvalue.
  2. Verify @thm-left-right-biorthogonal for these vectors, and rescale the left eigenvectors so that yiTvi=1.
  3. Hence write Ak as a combination of two rank-one matrices, and check the formula for k=0 and k=1.

exr-spectral-mapping-c1.title: C1: Traces of powers of AB and BA
exr-spectral-mapping-c1.title_html: C1: Traces of powers of AB and BA
exr-spectral-mapping-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×m(F).

  1. Prove that B(AB)k−1A=(BA)k for every k≥1, and deduce that tr((AB)k)=tr((BA)k).
  2. Now let F=C. Give a second proof of the trace identity from @thm-ab-ba-eigenvalues and @cor-trace-det-of-polynomial.

exr-spectral-mapping-c2.title: C2: Adding a commuting nilpotent matrix
exr-spectral-mapping-c2.title_html: C2: Adding a commuting nilpotent matrix
exr-spectral-mapping-c2.html:
Let A,N∈Mn(C), n≥1, with AN=NA and N nilpotent.

  1. Prove that pA+N=pA; in particular spec(A+N)=spec(A) and det(A+N)=detA.
  2. Deduce that if A is invertible, so is A+N.
  3. Show that (a) fails without AN=NA.

Hint: triangularize A and N together.

exr-spectral-mapping-c3.title: C3: How many traces, and which field?
exr-spectral-mapping-c3.title_html: C3: How many traces, and which field?
exr-spectral-mapping-c3.html:
1. Let ω=e2πi/3∈C and C=diag(1,ω,ω2). Show that trC=trC2=0 but C is not nilpotent. Explain why this does not contradict @thm-nilpotent-trace-powers.
  2. Let n≥2. Give a matrix C∈Mn(C) with trCk=0 for k=1,…,n−1 that is not nilpotent.
  3. Let A,B∈Mn(C) and suppose C=AB−BA commutes with A. Prove that Cn=0.
  4. Over F2, find a non-nilpotent C∈M2(F2) with trCk=0 for every k≥1.

exr-triangularization-a1.title: A1
exr-triangularization-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for A∈Mn(F) to be triangularizable over F.
  2. State the Triangularization Theorem.
  3. For a basis (v1,…,vn), which subspaces must be invariant for [T]B to be upper triangular?
  4. True or false: every A∈Mn(R) is triangularizable over R. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: every triangularizable matrix is diagonalizable. Justify your answer.
  6. Let A∈M4(C) have pA=(x−3)3(x+1). What are the diagonal entries of any upper triangular matrix similar to A, and what are trA and detA?

exr-triangularization-b1.title: B1: Triangularizing matrices
exr-triangularization-b1.html:
For each real matrix, find an invertible P such that P−1AP is upper triangular, and write down P−1AP.

  1. A=(31−11).
  2. A=(201131102), with pA=(x−1)(x−3)2 (@exm-charpoly-small).

exr-triangularization-b2.title: B2: Nilpotent matrices are strictly triangular
exr-triangularization-b2.title_html: B2: Nilpotent matrices are strictly triangular
exr-triangularization-b2.html: Let A∈Mn(C), n≥1, with Ak=0 for some k≥1. Prove that A is similar to a strictly upper triangular matrix, that is, an upper triangular matrix with zero diagonal.

exr-triangularization-b3.title: B3: Eigenvalues of powers from a triangular form
exr-triangularization-b3.title_html: B3: Eigenvalues of powers from a triangular form
exr-triangularization-b3.html:
Let A∈Mn(C), n≥1, and let P−1AP=U be upper triangular with diagonal entries d1,…,dn.

  1. Show that the product of two upper triangular matrices is upper triangular, with diagonal entries the products of the corresponding diagonal entries.
  2. Deduce that pAk=(x−d1k)⋯(x−dnk) and tr(Ak)=d1k+⋯+dnk for every k≥1.
  3. Suppose pA=(x−1)(x+1)(x−2). Find pA2, trA2 and detA2.

exr-triangularization-c1.title: C1: A second proof of Cayley–Hamilton
exr-triangularization-c1.title_html: C1: A second proof of Cayley–Hamilton
exr-triangularization-c1.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V) have a basis B=(v1,…,vn) with [T]B upper triangular, with diagonal entries d1,…,dn. Let U0={0} and Uk=span(v1,…,vk).

  1. Let Sk=(T−d1idV)(T−d2idV)⋯(T−dkidV). Prove by induction on k that Sk(Uk)={0} for 1≤k≤n.
  2. Deduce that pT(T)=0, without using the adjugate.
  3. Deduce the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem for every A∈Mn(C), and then for every A∈Mn(R).
  4. Why does this argument, on its own, not prove the theorem for A∈M2(F2) with pA=x2+x+1?

Hint: for (a), use the last statement of @thm-triangular-iff-flag.

exr-triangularization-c2.title: C2: Real operators have small invariant subspaces
exr-triangularization-c2.title_html: C2: Real operators have small invariant subspaces
exr-triangularization-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(R), n≥1, regarded also as a complex matrix.

  1. Let λ=a+bi (a,b∈R) be a complex eigenvalue of A with eigenvector z=x+iy, where x,y∈Rn. Show that Ax=ax−by and Ay=bx+ay.
  2. Deduce that span(x,y)⊆Rn is A-invariant, and has dimension 1 or 2.
  3. Deduce that every operator on a real vector space V with 1≤dim⁡V<∞ has an invariant subspace of dimension 1 or 2.
  4. For C=(00210−1012), check that z=(0,−2,1)+i(−2,1,0) is an eigenvector for i, and find the invariant plane of (b).

exr-triangularization-c3.title: C3: Traces of powers detect nilpotency
exr-triangularization-c3.title_html: C3: Traces of powers detect nilpotency
exr-triangularization-c3.html:
Let C∈Mn(C), n≥1, with tr(Ck)=0 for k=1,…,n. The goal is to prove that Cn=0.

  1. Let d1,…,dn be the diagonal entries of a triangular form of C. Show that d1k+⋯+dnk=0 for k=1,…,n.
  2. Suppose some di≠0. Let μ1,…,μr (r≥1) be the distinct non-zero values among the di, and let mj≥1 be the number of indices i with di=μj. Show that ∑j=1rmjμjk=0 for k=1,…,r.
  3. Show that the r×r matrix with (k,j)-entry μjk is invertible, and derive a contradiction from (b).
  4. Conclude that every di=0, that pC=xn, and that Cn=0.
  5. Show that the statement fails over F2.

Hint: for (c), factor the matrix as a transposed Vandermonde matrix times a diagonal matrix.

lem-invariance-on-spanning-list.title: Invariance Can Be Checked on a Spanning List
lem-invariance-on-spanning-list.title_html: Invariance Can Be Checked on a Spanning List
lem-invariance-on-spanning-list.html: Let T∈L(V) and U=span(u1,…,uk). Then U is T-invariant if and only if Tui∈U for each i=1,…,k.

lem-invariant-charpoly-splits.title: Restrictions and Quotients Inherit Splitting
lem-invariant-charpoly-splits.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, let T∈L(V), and let U be a T-invariant subspace with {0}≠U≠V. If pT splits over F, then pT|U and pT¯ split over F, where T¯ is the induced operator on V/U.

lem-monic-divisors.title: Monic Divisors of a Factored Polynomial
lem-monic-divisors.title_html: Monic Divisors of a Factored Polynomial
lem-monic-divisors.html: Let f=p1e1⋯pkek∈F[x], where k≥1, p1,…,pk are distinct monic irreducible polynomials and ei≥1. Then the monic divisors of f are exactly the polynomials p1f1⋯pkfkwith 0≤fi≤ei for each i.

prp-invariant-sum-intersection.title: Sums and Intersections of Invariant Subspaces
prp-invariant-sum-intersection.title_html: Sums and Intersections of Invariant Subspaces
prp-invariant-sum-intersection.html: Let T∈L(V) and let U1,…,Uk be T-invariant subspaces of V. Then U1+⋯+Uk and U1∩⋯∩Uk are T-invariant.

prp-left-eigenvectors-transpose.title: Left Eigenvectors Are Eigenvectors of the Transpose
prp-left-eigenvectors-transpose.title_html: Left Eigenvectors Are Eigenvectors of the Transpose
prp-left-eigenvectors-transpose.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) and λ∈F.

  1. y is a left eigenvector of A for λ if and only if y is an eigenvector of AT for λ.
  2. A has a left eigenvector for λ if and only if λ∈spec(A). Moreover pAT=pA, and aAT(λ)=aA(λ), gAT(λ)=gA(λ).

prp-left-right-eigen-expansion.title: Expansion in Left and Right Eigenvectors
prp-left-right-eigen-expansion.title_html: Expansion in Left and Right Eigenvectors
prp-left-right-eigen-expansion.html:
Let A=PDP−1 with P∈Mn(F) invertible and D=diag(λ1,…,λn). Let v1,…,vn be the columns of P, and let y1T,…,ynT be the rows of P−1. Then:

  1. vi is a right eigenvector and yi a left eigenvector of A for λi;
  2. yiTvj=1 if i=j and 0 if i≠j;
  3. for every q∈F[x], q(A)=∑i=1nq(λi)viyiT,in particularAk=∑i=1nλikviyiT(k∈N).

prp-minimal-polynomial-block-diagonal.title: Minimal Polynomial of a Block Diagonal Matrix
prp-minimal-polynomial-block-diagonal.title_html: Minimal Polynomial of a Block Diagonal Matrix
prp-minimal-polynomial-block-diagonal.html: Let A∈Mk(F) and B∈Ml(F) with k,l≥1. Then mA⊕B=lcm(mA,mB).

prp-minimal-polynomial-first-dependence.title: The First Dependence Among the Powers
prp-minimal-polynomial-first-dependence.title_html: The First Dependence Among the Powers
prp-minimal-polynomial-first-dependence.html: Let V be finite-dimensional and T∈L(V). Let d≥0 be the least integer such that the list (idV,T,…,Td) in L(V) is linearly dependent. Then there are unique c0,…,cd−1∈F with Td=c0idV+c1T+⋯+cd−1Td−1, and mT=xd−cd−1xd−1−⋯−c1x−c0. In particular deg⁡mT=d. The same holds for A∈Mn(F), with powers of A in Mn(F).

prp-multiplicities-similarity-invariant.title: Similar Matrices Have the Same Multiplicities
prp-multiplicities-similarity-invariant.title_html: Similar Matrices Have the Same Multiplicities
prp-multiplicities-similarity-invariant.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) with A∼B, and let λ∈F. Then aA(λ)=aB(λ) and gA(λ)=gB(λ).

prp-one-dimensional-invariant.title: Invariant Lines
prp-one-dimensional-invariant.html: Let T∈L(V) and v∈V with v≠0. Then span(v) is T-invariant if and only if Tv=λv for some λ∈F.

prp-stochastic-properties.title: Basic Properties of Stochastic Matrices
prp-stochastic-properties.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(R) be stochastic and x∈Rn a probability vector. Then:

  1. Ax is a probability vector;
  2. AB is stochastic, and so is Ak for every k∈N;
  3. 1 is a left eigenvector of A for the eigenvalue 1; in particular 1∈spec(A).

thm-ab-ba-eigenvalues.title: AB and BA Have the Same Non-zero Eigenvalues
thm-ab-ba-eigenvalues.title_html: AB and BA Have the Same Non-zero Eigenvalues
thm-ab-ba-eigenvalues.html:
Let m,n≥1, A∈Mm×n(F) and B∈Mn×m(F). Then xnpAB(x)=xmpBA(x). Consequently:

  1. for every λ≠0 in F, aAB(λ)=aBA(λ); in particular AB and BA have the same non-zero eigenvalues;
  2. if m=n, then pAB=pBA; and if m≥n, then pAB=xm−npBA.

thm-cayley-hamilton.title: Cayley–Hamilton Theorem
thm-cayley-hamilton.html: Let n≥1 and A∈Mn(F). Then pA(A)=0. Likewise, if V is a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V≥1 and T∈L(V), then pT(T)=0.

thm-commuting-common-eigenvector.title: Commuting Operators Have a Common Eigenvector
thm-commuting-common-eigenvector.title_html: Commuting Operators Have a Common Eigenvector
thm-commuting-common-eigenvector.html: Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and let F⊆L(V) be a non-empty commuting family such that pT splits over F for every T∈F. Then there is a non-zero v∈V that is an eigenvector of every T∈F. This applies to every commuting family when F=C.

thm-commuting-preserves-eigenspaces.title: Commuting Operators Preserve Eigenspaces
thm-commuting-preserves-eigenspaces.html: Let V be a vector space over F, and let S,T∈L(V) with ST=TS. Then for every λ∈F, the eigenspace Eλ(T) is S-invariant.

thm-complex-operator-has-eigenvalue.title: Complex Operators Have Eigenvalues
thm-complex-operator-has-eigenvalue.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over C with V≠{0}, and let T∈L(V). Then T has an eigenvalue. The same holds for every A∈Mn(C) with n≥1.

thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form.title: The Diagonal of a Triangular Form
thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form.title_html: The Diagonal of a Triangular Form
thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=n≥1, T∈L(V), and let B be a basis with [T]B upper triangular, with diagonal entries d1,…,dn. Then:

  1. pT=(x−d1)(x−d2)⋯(x−dn);
  2. spec(T)={d1,…,dn}, and each eigenvalue λ occurs among d1,…,dn exactly aT(λ) times;
  3. trT=d1+⋯+dn and detT=d1⋯dn.

In particular, any two triangular forms of T have the same diagonal entries, up to order.

thm-diagonalizable-iff-minimal-distinct-.title: Diagonalizability via the Minimal Polynomial
thm-diagonalizable-iff-minimal-distinct-.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V≥1, and let T∈L(V). The following are equivalent:

  1. T is diagonalizable;
  2. mT=(x−λ1)(x−λ2)⋯(x−λk) for some distinct λ1,…,λk∈F, that is, mT splits over F with no repeated root;
  3. some polynomial (x−μ1)⋯(x−μr) with distinct μ1,…,μr∈F annihilates T.

In that case λ1,…,λk are the distinct eigenvalues of T. The same holds for A∈Mn(F).

thm-diagonalization.title: Diagonalization Theorem
thm-diagonalization.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, let T∈L(V), and let λ1,…,λk be the distinct eigenvalues of T (possibly k=0). The following are equivalent:

  1. T is diagonalizable;
  2. V has a basis consisting of eigenvectors of T;
  3. V=Eλ1(T)⊕⋯⊕Eλk(T);
  4. dim⁡Eλ1(T)+⋯+dim⁡Eλk(T)=n;
  5. pT splits over F, and gT(λi)=aT(λi) for every i=1,…,k.

In that case, if B is a basis of eigenvectors, then [T]B is diagonal, its diagonal entries are the eigenvalues of the corresponding basis vectors, and each λi appears on the diagonal exactly aT(λi)=gT(λi) times.

thm-direct-sum-invariant-block-diagonal.title: Invariant Direct Sums and Block Diagonal Matrices
thm-direct-sum-invariant-block-diagonal.title_html: Invariant Direct Sums and Block Diagonal Matrices
thm-direct-sum-invariant-block-diagonal.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with V=U1⊕⋯⊕Uk, where each Ui≠{0} has a basis Bi of length ni. Let B be the list B1,…,Bk written one after another, and T∈L(V). Then B is a basis of V, and the following are equivalent:

  1. each Ui is T-invariant;
  2. [T]B is block diagonal with respect to the partition n1,…,nk.

In that case [T]B=[T|U1]B1⊕⋯⊕[T|Uk]Bk,pT=pT|U1⋯pT|Uk.

thm-distinct-eigenvalues-independent.title: Distinct Eigenvalues Give Independent Eigenvectors
thm-distinct-eigenvalues-independent.html: Let T∈L(V), let λ1,…,λk∈F be distinct eigenvalues of T, and for each i let vi be an eigenvector of T for λi. Then (v1,…,vk) is linearly independent.

thm-eigenvalue-characterizations.title: Characterizations of Eigenvalues
thm-eigenvalue-characterizations.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, let T∈L(V) and λ∈F. The following are equivalent:

  1. λ is an eigenvalue of T;
  2. Eλ(T)≠{0}, that is, T−λidV is not injective;
  3. T−λidV is not invertible;
  4. det(λidV−T)=0;
  5. pT(λ)=0.

In particular T has at most n eigenvalues. For A∈Mn(F): λ is an eigenvalue of A if and only if pA(λ)=0, if and only if λI−A is not invertible.

thm-geometric-le-algebraic.title: Geometric Multiplicity Is at Most Algebraic Multiplicity
thm-geometric-le-algebraic.title_html: Geometric Multiplicity Is at Most Algebraic Multiplicity
thm-geometric-le-algebraic.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, let T∈L(V), and let λ∈F be an eigenvalue of T. Then 1≤gT(λ)≤aT(λ).

thm-invariant-subspace-matrix.title: Invariant Subspaces and Block Triangular Matrices
thm-invariant-subspace-matrix.title_html: Invariant Subspaces and Block Triangular Matrices
thm-invariant-subspace-matrix.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional, T∈L(V), and U a subspace with {0}≠U≠V. Let BU=(u1,…,uk) be a basis of U, extended to a basis B=(u1,…,uk,w1,…,wl) of V, and put B¯=(w1+U,…,wl+U).

  1. U is T-invariant if and only if [T]B has zero lower-left l×k block.
  2. In that case [T]B=([T|U]BUB0[T¯]B¯) for some B∈Mk×l(F), and detT=det(T|U)detT¯,pT=pT|UpT¯.

thm-invertible-tfae-eigen.title: Invertible Matrix Theorem, with Eigenvalues
thm-invertible-tfae-eigen.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) with n≥1. The following are equivalent, and each is equivalent to each of the conditions of @thm-invertible-tfae-det and @thm-invertible-tfae.

  1. A is invertible.
  2. 0 is not an eigenvalue of A, that is, 0∉spec(A).

Likewise, an operator T on a finite-dimensional space V≠{0} is invertible if and only if 0∉spec(T).

thm-left-right-biorthogonal.title: Left and Right Eigenvectors Are Biorthogonal
thm-left-right-biorthogonal.title_html: Left and Right Eigenvectors Are Biorthogonal
thm-left-right-biorthogonal.html: Let A∈Mn(F), let y be a left eigenvector of A for μ, and let v be a right eigenvector of A for λ. If λ≠μ, then yTv=0.

thm-linear-recurrence-solution.title: Solving a Diagonalizable Recurrence
thm-linear-recurrence-solution.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be diagonalizable, with A=PDP−1, D=diag(λ1,…,λn), and let v1,…,vn be the columns of P. Let x0∈Fn, and let (c1,…,cn)=P−1x0, so that x0=c1v1+⋯+cnvn. Then the sequence defined by xk+1=Axk is xk=Akx0=c1λ1kv1+c2λ2kv2+⋯+cnλnkvn(k∈N).

thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable.title: Long-Run Behavior of a Diagonalizable Markov Chain
thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable.title_html: Long-Run Behavior of a Diagonalizable Markov Chain
thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable.html:
Let A∈Mn(R), n≥1, be stochastic. Suppose that A is diagonalizable over C, that aA(1)=1, and that every other eigenvalue λ∈C of A has |λ|<1. Then:

  1. A has exactly one steady state v;
  2. Ak→v1T entrywise as k→∞;
  3. for every probability vector x0, the Markov chain xk=Akx0 converges entrywise to v.

thm-minimal-polynomial-divides.title: Annihilating Polynomials Are Multiples of the Minimal Polynomial
thm-minimal-polynomial-divides.title_html: Annihilating Polynomials Are Multiples of the Minimal Polynomial
thm-minimal-polynomial-divides.html: Let V be finite-dimensional and T∈L(V). For every p∈F[x], p(T)=0⟺mT∣p. In particular, a non-zero polynomial that annihilates T has degree at least deg⁡mT. If V≠{0}, then deg⁡mT≥1.

thm-minimal-polynomial-roots.title: Roots of the Minimal Polynomial
thm-minimal-polynomial-roots.html: Let V be finite-dimensional, T∈L(V) and λ∈F. Then mT(λ)=0 if and only if λ is an eigenvalue of T. Consequently, if dim⁡V≥1, then mT and pT have the same roots in F.

thm-minimal-polynomial-similarity.title: Similar Matrices Have the Same Minimal Polynomial
thm-minimal-polynomial-similarity.title_html: Similar Matrices Have the Same Minimal Polynomial
thm-minimal-polynomial-similarity.html: Let V be finite-dimensional with a basis B, and let T∈L(V). Then mT=m[T]B. If A,B∈Mn(F) are similar, then mA=mB.

thm-nilpotent-trace-powers.title: Nilpotent Matrices via Eigenvalues and Traces
thm-nilpotent-trace-powers.title_html: Nilpotent Matrices via Eigenvalues and Traces
thm-nilpotent-trace-powers.html:
Let n≥1 and A∈Mn(C). The following are equivalent:

  1. A is nilpotent, that is, As=0 for some s≥1;
  2. spec(A)={0};
  3. pA=xn;
  4. An=0;
  5. trAk=0 for k=1,2,…,n.

The same holds for A∈Mn(F) when F is a subfield of C, such as Q or R, with spec(A) in (b) taken over C.

thm-powers-diagonalizable.title: Powers and Polynomials of a Diagonalizable Matrix
thm-powers-diagonalizable.title_html: Powers and Polynomials of a Diagonalizable Matrix
thm-powers-diagonalizable.html: Let A=PDP−1 with P∈Mn(F) invertible and D=diag(d1,…,dn). Then for every k∈N and every p∈F[x], Ak=Pdiag(d1k,…,dnk)P−1,p(A)=Pdiag(p(d1),…,p(dn))P−1. If moreover every di≠0, then A is invertible and A−1=Pdiag(d1−1,…,dn−1)P−1.

thm-primary-decomposition.title: Primary Decomposition Theorem
thm-primary-decomposition.html:
Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, let T∈L(V), and let mT=p1e1⋯pkek, where p1,…,pk are distinct monic irreducible polynomials and ei≥1. Put Vi:=kerpi(T)ei(i=1,…,k). Then:

  1. V=V1⊕V2⊕⋯⊕Vk;
  2. each Vi is T-invariant and non-zero;
  3. the restriction T|Vi has minimal polynomial mT|Vi=piei;
  4. for each i there is hi∈F[x] such that hi(T) is the projection of V onto Vi along ⨁j≠iVj.

thm-real-matrix-complex-eigenvalues.title: Complex Eigenvalues of Real Matrices Come in Conjugate Pairs
thm-real-matrix-complex-eigenvalues.title_html: Complex Eigenvalues of Real Matrices Come in Conjugate Pairs
thm-real-matrix-complex-eigenvalues.html:
Let A∈Mn(R), regarded as an element of Mn(C). If λ∈C is an eigenvalue of A with eigenvector v∈Cn, then λ― is an eigenvalue of A with eigenvector v―, the vector of conjugated entries. Moreover:

  1. multλ(pA)=multλ―(pA);
  2. if λ∉R, then (v,v―) is linearly independent over C.

thm-scalar-recurrence-distinct-roots.title: Scalar Recurrences with Distinct Roots
thm-scalar-recurrence-distinct-roots.html: Let n≥1, c0,…,cn−1∈F, and suppose p=xn+cn−1xn−1+⋯+c0 has n distinct roots λ1,…,λn∈F. Then a sequence (ak)k∈N in F satisfies (∗) if and only if there are b1,…,bn∈F with ak=b1λ1k+b2λ2k+⋯+bnλnkfor every k∈N. In that case b1,…,bn are uniquely determined by the initial values a0,…,an−1.

thm-simultaneous-diagonalization.title: Simultaneous Diagonalization
thm-simultaneous-diagonalization.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V≥1, and let S,T∈L(V) be diagonalizable. Then S and T are simultaneously diagonalizable if and only if ST=TS.

For matrices: if A,B∈Mn(F) are diagonalizable over F, there is an invertible P∈Mn(F) with P−1AP and P−1BP both diagonal if and only if AB=BA.

thm-simultaneous-diagonalization-family.title: Simultaneous Diagonalization of a Commuting Family
thm-simultaneous-diagonalization-family.title_html: Simultaneous Diagonalization of a Commuting Family
thm-simultaneous-diagonalization-family.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V≥1, and let F⊆L(V) be a family of diagonalizable operators. Then F is simultaneously diagonalizable if and only if it is commuting.

thm-simultaneous-triangularization.title: Simultaneous Triangularization
thm-simultaneous-triangularization.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let F⊆L(V) be a non-empty commuting family such that pT splits over F for every T∈F. Then there is one basis B of V such that [T]B is upper triangular for every T∈F.

In particular, if A1,…,Ar∈Mn(C) commute pairwise, there is an invertible P∈Mn(C) such that P−1AiP is upper triangular for every i.

thm-spectral-mapping.title: Spectral Mapping Theorem
thm-spectral-mapping.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V). Suppose pT splits over F, say pT(x)=(x−λ1)(x−λ2)⋯(x−λn), where each eigenvalue appears as often as its algebraic multiplicity. Then for every q∈F[x], pq(T)(x)=(x−q(λ1))(x−q(λ2))⋯(x−q(λn)), and consequently spec(q(T))=q(spec(T))={q(λ):λ∈spec(T)}. In particular this holds for every operator on a non-zero finite-dimensional complex space, and for every A∈Mn(C).

thm-trace-det-eigenvalues.title: Trace and Determinant from Eigenvalues
thm-trace-det-eigenvalues.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V). Suppose pT splits over F, and let λ1,…,λk be the distinct eigenvalues of T. Then a(λ1)+⋯+a(λk)=n,trT=∑i=1ka(λi)λi,detT=∏i=1kλia(λi). In words: listing each eigenvalue as often as its algebraic multiplicity, the trace is the sum of the list and the determinant is its product. In particular this holds for every operator on a non-zero finite-dimensional complex space, and for every A∈Mn(C).

thm-triangular-iff-flag.title: Triangular Matrices and Chains of Invariant Subspaces
thm-triangular-iff-flag.title_html: Triangular Matrices and Chains of Invariant Subspaces
thm-triangular-iff-flag.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional with basis B=(v1,…,vn), let T∈L(V), and put U0={0} and Uk=span(v1,…,vk) for 1≤k≤n. The following are equivalent:

  1. [T]B is upper triangular;
  2. Tvk∈Uk for every k=1,…,n;
  3. each Uk is T-invariant.

In that case, if d1,…,dn are the diagonal entries of [T]B, then (T−dkidV)(Uk)⊆Uk−1 for every k.

thm-triangularization.title: Triangularization Theorem
thm-triangularization.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V). Then T is triangularizable over F if and only if pT splits over F. The same holds for A∈Mn(F) and pA.
